blocks.content: 1. Cell – Definition and Discovery

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The cell is the basic structural, functional, and biological unit of all known living organisms.
Robert Hooke discovered cells in 1665 by observing cork slice under a primitive microscope.
Cell Theory was proposed by Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann, and extended by Rudolf Virchow.
Cells are broadly categorized into Prokaryotic (lacking true nucleus) and Eukaryotic (having membrane-bound nucleus).
Cell membrane is selectively permeable, controlling the movement of substances in and out of the cell.
Cell organelles like mitochondria, ribosomes, nucleus, and cytoplasm carry out specific vital cellular functions.

blocks.content:
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.

All living organisms are made up of one or more cells.

Cells perform all vital life processes such as respiration, metabolism, growth, and reproduction.

The term ‘cell’ was first used by Robert Hooke in 1665 while observing cork under a microscope.

He described cells as empty box-like structures.

Later scientists discovered living cells and their internal components.

This discovery laid the foundation of modern Biology.
2. Cell Theory

Cell Theory was proposed by Schleiden and Schwann.

According to the Cell Theory:

• All living organisms are composed of cells.

• The cell is the basic unit of structure and function.

• All cells arise from pre-existing cells (added by Rudolf Virchow).

This theory established that life originates at the cellular level.

It explains growth, reproduction, and repair in living organisms.
3. Types of Cells

Cells are classified into two major types based on the presence of nucleus.

Prokaryotic cells lack a well-defined nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

Examples include bacteria and blue-green algae.

Eukaryotic cells have a true nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.

Examples include plant and animal cells.

Prokaryotic cells are smaller and simpler, whereas eukaryotic cells are larger and complex.
4. Cell Shape and Size
CHAPTER 2: CELL – STRUCTURE AND FUNCTIONS

Cells differ widely in shape and size depending upon their function.

The smallest living cells are Mycoplasma.

The largest cell in the living world is the egg of an ostrich.

The longest cells in the human body are nerve cells.

Red blood cells are biconcave in shape to increase surface area for oxygen transport.

Cell size is measured in micrometers.
5. Structure of a Cell . Cell Theory

A typical cell consists of three main parts: cell membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus.

The cell membrane encloses the cell and regulates movement of substances.

Cytoplasm is the site of metabolic activities.

The nucleus controls cellular functions and contains genetic material.

Plant cells also have a cell wall and plastids.
6. Cell Membrane

The cell membrane is a selectively permeable membrane made of phospholipids and proteins.

It allows diffusion and osmosis.

It maintains internal balance of the cell.

Carbon dioxide and oxygen pass through the membrane by diffusion.

Water moves through the membrane by osmosis.
7. Cytoplasm

Cytoplasm is a jelly-like fluid inside the cell membrane.

It contains enzymes, water, and cell organelles.

Most biochemical reactions occur in the cytoplasm.

It helps in intracellular transport and supports organelles.
8. Cell Organelles

Cell organelles are specialized structures performing specific functions.

Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell and produce ATP.

Ribosomes synthesize proteins.

Endoplasmic reticulum helps in synthesis and transport of proteins and lipids.

Golgi apparatus packages proteins.

Lysosomes digest waste materials and are called suicidal bags.

Plastids are found in plant cells only.

Vacuoles store food and waste materials.

items: Rudolf Virchow added the phrase 'Omnis cellula-e-cellula' (all cells arise from pre-existing cells) to the Cell Theory.
Mitochondria are known as the 'Powerhouse of the Cell' because they produce energy in the form of ATP.
Lysosomes are called 'Suicidal Bags' due to the presence of digestive enzymes that break down worn-out cell parts.
Ribosomes are non-membrane bound organelles responsible for protein synthesis in both prokaryotes and eukaryotes.

blocks.content: 9. Nucleus

The nucleus is a membrane-bound organelle present in eukaryotic cells.

It contains chromatin made of DNA and proteins.

Chromatin condenses into chromosomes during cell division.

Genes are located on chromosomes.

Some cells like mature red blood cells lack a nucleus.
10. IMPORTANT FACTS ( FOCUS)

• Cells were discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665.

• Smallest living cell – Mycoplasma.

• Largest cell – Ostrich egg.

• Longest cell – Nerve cell.

• RBCs do not have nucleus in mammals.

• Mitochondria contain their own DNA.

• Ribosomes are non-membrane bound organelles.

• Lysosomes are called suicidal bags.

• Cell membrane is selectively permeable.

• Plant cells have cell wall and plastids.

• Prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles.
